overview: Bagirmi developed southeast of Lake Chad around Massenya in the sixteenth century. Its rulers negotiated, fought and sometimes paid tribute to Bornu and Wadai. Both Bagirmi labels on this map refer to phases of this kingdom, with imperfect imported borders.

periods.title: An Islamic court develops
periods.summary: Sultan Abdullah adopted Islam in the later sixteenth century, while older beliefs continued among the population.

periods.title: Regional rivalry and colonial rule
periods.summary: Raids, tribute and invasion linked Bagirmi to its neighbors. French treaties in 1897 and 1903 curtailed its independence.

items.text: Bagirmi’s rulers used the title mbang. Conversion at court did not make the entire population religiously uniform. Bornu’s influence included scholars as well as armies, and periods of tribute alternated with renewed independence.

In the eighteenth century Bagirmi raided southern and southeastern communities and profited from selling captives. Later invasions also carried Bagirmi’s own inhabitants into slavery. Royal prosperity and ordinary people’s security could move in opposite directions.

Historian Viviana Pâques compared oral traditions and written evidence during research in 1966 and 1967. The sources did not always agree on reigns or dates. A royal list is historical evidence to investigate, rather than a ready-made calendar immune to disagreement.

sections.title: A capital of earth and brick

items.text: Archaeologist Annie Lebeuf located the old capital, Boum Massenya, east of the Chari. By her 1967 report, its great earth enclosure survived as a low, uneven trace. An almost vanished wall can still reveal where a city once organized its defenses.

Fired-brick remains marked the palace, mosque and houses of prominent residents. Some old bricks had been reused for road fill. Archaeologists therefore had to read both surviving buildings and displaced materials, rather than expecting a complete abandoned city waiting untouched.

Lebeuf describes Massenya chiefly as a royal and administrative centre. A capital need not also be the kingdom’s busiest trading town. Its palace and officials gave it importance even when the most active buying and selling happened elsewhere.

In 1898 Sultan Gaorang ordered the old capital burned and abandoned as Rabih threatened it. The later settlement called Massenya occupied a different location. Keeping those places separate helps explain why a modern town and an archaeological capital share a name.

In 1852 Barth met Faki Sambo, a blind Fula scholar educated at al-Azhar in Cairo. They discussed books and distant places. The encounter connects a Bagirmi scholarly household with an intellectual network stretching well beyond the Lake Chad region.

Sambo served Barth a cold rice pudding with dates from Kanem; Barth offered coffee. Manuscripts and conversation shared the scene with refreshments. Even a meeting that later becomes historical evidence may have begun with something good to eat.

Barth described weavers and dyers, including Kanuri craftspeople producing dark cloth. His account also names officials responsible for pasture, woods and waters. Running a kingdom involved regulating useful resources as well as issuing commands at court.

Barth recorded the language name as “tar Bágrimma”. This is his nineteenth-century Roman transcription, not a surviving text written by a Bagirmi court scribe. It offers a small linguistic trace alongside the much richer spoken knowledge of the people he met.

A modern Bagirmi book supplies an attested writing sample: “Kup an Duniya”, translated by its publisher as “The Beginning of Creation”. This illustrated Christian publication demonstrates continuing use of the language in print; it is not a text from the Muslim sultanate.

ending.text: French protection in 1897 and further restrictions in 1903 ended Bagirmi’s independent position. Its rulers continued under colonial control, and Bagirmi communities remained part of the region’s history. Neither imported map cutoff marks their disappearance.
